## What you take with you {.smaller}

<!-- The first line differs by format, keyed on the deck map in the YAML of
     each deck. -->

::: {.small}
- **Yours now**: [a reproduced result; an estimand statement and a causal graph that you wrote yourself; your results on the class chart, with a reason for each choice]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.methods"}[a reproduced result; an estimand statement; the place of your own specification on the curve of `r nrow(curve)`]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.short"}[a reproduced result; an estimand statement; a preregistration block that you filled in before any result existed]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.open-science"}[R code that reproduces a published result; a report whose numbers come from that code; a map of the toolchain]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.data-tools"}
- **Read**: the three *Nature* 2026 papers [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial]; the glossary [@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms]; @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand; on conditioning among replies, @MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment and @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias; on names in audits, @Gaddis2017HowBlackAre; and the paper itself [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]
- **Explore**: the case study, the decision map and the companion modules on the course site; the public data on the Dataverse; the SCORE dossier on the OSF
- **Keep going locally**: the research-software and open-research teams at your university, or a ReproducibiliTea journal club near you
- Everything is on the course site, and everything is open – fork any of it
:::

::: notes
[You take home a reproduced result, an estimand statement and a causal graph that you wrote for a real published claim, and your results on the class chart, each with a reason.]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.methods"}[You take home a reproduced result, an estimand statement for a real published claim, and the place of your own choice among every justifiable analysis of its data.]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.short"}[You take home a reproduced result, an estimand statement for a real published claim, and a preregistration that you filled in before any result existed.]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.open-science"}[You take home code that reproduces a published result, a report in which every number comes from that code, and a map of the tools that make both possible.]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.data-tools"} The reading list on the slide is short on purpose: the three Nature papers on reproduction, robustness and replication, the glossary that gave us the grid, the paper on estimands, two short papers on why comparing among replies is risky in an audit experiment, one on how names are read, and the original paper. The course site has the case study, the decision map, the companion modules and the full public record. And two pointers for keeping the habit alive: most universities have a research-software team and an open-research or library data service that run training like this, and ReproducibiliTea journal clubs meet in many cities.
:::
